title: Why Did Soda Can Rings Disappear?

fin.small: Sources: E. C. Fraze, US Patent 3,255,917, 1966; D. F. Cudzik / Reynolds Metals, US Patent 3,836,038 'Easy-open wall', 1974; Wikipedia, 'Drink can'.

parts: Old soda cans had a ring you pulled clean off. Today the tab stays on. Why?
Stay to the end for the reason written in the patent itself.
In 1963, Ermal Fraze of Ohio filed a patent: a tab riveted to a strip of the lid.
You pulled, and the whole strip came off in your hand.
Then that sharp little strip had to go somewhere.
So why did the ring disappear?
In 1972, Daniel Cudzik at Reynolds Metals filed a new design.
You lift the tab, it pushes the panel inside, and nothing comes off the can.
His patent says why: tossed strips were a litter problem, and barefoot people on beaches got serious cuts.
Who had the idea first is still argued. This patent shows what it was meant to fix.
Our reading: that tab is a safety fix you use every day. Subscribe for the next one.
